      Your new storage ottoman

      Yours is 75 square and 44 high, in blue cord42. No navy cord storage ottoman is made that size71, so the plan's is navy velvet.

      • Our pick: ISTOOLS Large Velvet Storage Ottoman, 76 × 76, navy68. It's the nearest size made to yours (1 cm wider each way), with a padded lid that lifts off, a box inside for your games and cards, and a wooden frame on short legs. They don't publish its height (we've drawn 45) and the price varies by size and colour (about £300 at 76): check both on the listing before ordering.
      • Smaller and cheaper: Dunelm Square Opulent Velvet Storage Footstool, navy, 62 × 62 × 39, 18 deep inside, £139–19969. It gives 14 cm back each way.
      • Bigger: Dunelm Zoe Pinstripe Square Storage Footstool, 96 × 96 × 49, navy, £99.50–19970. It's a coffee-table size, and too big for the gap beside your coffee table.

      Your games and cards in it. Inside it is about 70 square and 28 deep (as drawn; check the real one when it comes).       The record table

      Your coffee table's 90 × 50, from two IKEA KALLAX80 on their backs: two bins of LPs, spine-up, about 80 in each. An oak lid lifts on a piano hinge along the TV side; it rolls on castors. 48.5 high.

      • Buy: two KALLAX 42 × 42 (£19 each)80; an 18 mm oak board, 60 × 12081; 12 mm ply82; four 50 mm castors, 50 kg each83; a piano hinge cut to 8349; two lid stays84.
      • Make: build both KALLAX and screw them together side by side. Screw the ply (84 × 41) to the open backs; a castor 4 in from each corner.
      • The lid: the oak cut to 90 × 50, corners rounded, oiled; hinged to the TV side's top edge, 3.5 over each end; a stay each end, stopping at about 80°.
      • Check: loaded, about 65 kg; the castors take 200. The records stand on the ply, not the KALLAX shelves.

      The C-table

      At the sofa's open end: an oak top 45 × 30 at 62, reaching 12 over the seat. Your sofa sits on the floor, so no foot can slide under it as a bought one's does109; a 6 mm steel plate107 weighs its foot down instead. It holds about 12.1 kg on its far edge108. About £8–15.

      • Cut: from the Snowdon pack's second 18 mm board81: the top 45 × 30, the upright 45 × 57.5, the foot 45 × 21.
      • Make: glue and screw the upright to the top's and the foot's outer edges (three 40 mm screws each, plugged); round the corners; hardwax oil. Screw the plate under the foot, felt under the plate.
      • Check: it stands square; with a full mug on the far edge it doesn't rock.

      Built to your alcove: 186 wide, 38 deep, 235 to the ceiling

      • Base: 3 cm filler, three 60 cm bays, 3 cm filler. Bays 1 and 2 are IKEA BESTÅ 60×40×64 frames on a 9 cm plinth (tops at 73, back panels off); bay 3 is an 18 mm ply carcass 60 × 40 × 73 from the floor, split by a 12 mm divider into the slim game column (two face-out game drawers and the pads drawer) and the LP column (two face-out LP crates) under the turntable. One oak face frame runs across all three; its bottom rail hides the plinth and a hidden drawer under bay 2 with a finger pull (no push-to-open at floor level).
      • Depth: 40 cm frames, a 4 cm cable channel behind and the 2 cm face frame make 46 cm from the back wall, 8 cm proud of the chimney breast.
      • Worktop: solid oak, 186 × 46 × 3, top at 76, with a brush-lined slot behind the TV and a grommet behind the deck.
      • Oak uprights: 4.5 × 30 cm, 159 cm from the worktop to the ceiling. The left one is at 50.5–55, between the turntable zone and the TV. The right one stands against the breast at 181.5–186, a corner post that frames the TV. That leaves 126.5 cm between them, 2.15 cm clear of the TV each side.
      • TV: centre 118.25 cm from the side wall, in line with the sofa, on LG's stand set 2 cm off the back wall: bottom 81.4, centre 116.5, top 151.7. The soundbar sits centred under it at the worktop's front edge.
      • The turntable zone: 50.5 cm between the side wall and the left upright. The deck sits on the worktop with 2.65 cm each side and its lid opens to about 121. Above it is an oak shelf at 134, through-tenoned into the upright, carrying the Series X on its fan stand; the phono preamp hangs underneath at the back.
      • Shelves above: the record ledge at 155.4 between the uprights, four LPs face-out; the high shelf at 196, wall to wall in two lengths, with books, a box, a print, a small framed sleeve and Deco B.
      • Bay 2 with the sub: the PS3 keeps the top row. Below its shelf the bay splits: on the left the sub's column, 23.4 cm wide, then a 12 mm ply divider, then 32.2 cm for the PS2 over the PS1 on a part shelf. The sub stands on a 3 cm isolation riser with 1 cm each side and 2.9 above. Its front is flush with the face frame, so its driver faces the room and its rear port has 15.6 cm to the wall.
      • Power: the side-wall socket in front of the records bay becomes a double. Its two leads enter through a notch at the left end of the face frame's bottom rail and run back through the plinth to the channel.
      The media wall, looked over again
      • The TV's remote: the soundbar's top is 0.6 above the screen's bottom edge, right where LG puts the remote's receiver. Sit the bar 2 cm proud of the stand's foot so the beam from the sofa clears it; LG's Magic Remote works by radio once paired, so it doesn't mind either way (a check in the fit proof).
      • Heat: every console bay is open front and back, the bricks lie flat at the back with nothing on top, and the Series X has 15 cm each side and 21 above.
      • One remote for most of it: HDMI-CEC (SIMPLINK) lets the TV's remote work the soundbar and the modern consoles (step 13); the HDMI switch has its own remote for the retro side.

      The sub in the media wall

      You asked for the sub back in the unit, with the Xbox bricks moved behind. It fits, and it sits in the best spot for it: under the TV, beside the soundbar, so the bass comes from the same place as the picture. Here's how the base makes room, and what was checked.

      • The bricks go to the back. The Xbox One's brick (17 × 7.5 × 4.811) and the Xbox 360's (allowed 21 × 10 × 616) lie flat at the back of their shelves, by the channel's power leads. Microsoft asks for a ventilated space, flat on the rubber pads, with nothing on top26; the bays are open front and back.
      • That frees bay 1's fronts beside the two Xboxes, so the HDMI switch (beside the Xbox One, where its remote reaches it) and the RetroTINK (beside the Xbox 360) move up from bay 2.
      • Bay 2's lower half becomes two columns: the sub on the left, under the TV, and the PS2 over the PS1 on the right. The sub is 21.4 × 30.4 × 29.43; its column is 23.4 wide and 35.3 tall.
      • The port: the sub's front sits flush with the face frame, so its rear port is 15.6 cm from the wall through the open back and the channel. That's inside the 15–30 cm advised for a rear port25, at the low end, so the channel behind bay 2 stays clear: Switch 2 and the retro 6-way move behind bay 1.
      • Vibration, the one thing to test: Microsoft advises keeping the Xbox 360 away from subwoofers27, and the deck shares the worktop. The 360 is a whole bay away, the sub stands on an isolation riser without touching the divider or the frame, and the deck has isolation feet. Once it's built, play a disc game and a record at film volume. If anything skips, turn the sub down for that source; if it still does, the sub can go back under the dining wall.
      • The dining wall is clear underneath: no cover to make, and nothing to move for eight at the table.

      The fit proof: every item against its published size

      Each zone lists what goes in it, its size and its source (Fit proof), the space, what's left and a verdict. 92 of the 126 checks fit outright and none fail; 22 are tight, most of them snug by design; 12 need a check on site (the TV's plugs, the RetroTINK's size, the sub's vibration, the soundbar and the TV's remote eye, the stairs wall, and your shelf's height).

      Every zone's checks, with a filter for the tight ones, are in the Fit proof.

      Safety

      • Wall cabinets, shoe cabinets, the bar and the media wall: fix each to the wall with the anti-tip fittings for a solid wall; IKEA's own listings say they must be anchored.
      • Drilling: check for pipes and cables with a detector before every hole; the side wall carries the PC's leads.
      • The step drawers: a bearer under each tread once its riser is cut out: a joiner's job, or build them into the new stairs.
      • An old textured (Artex) ceiling: if it's older than about 2000, have it tested for asbestos before sanding, drilling or skimming it.
      • Mains electrics: the sockets and the light fittings: done to Part P, or by an electrician.
      • The dining table: never swing it up or down with anything on it; check all four legs have clicked before you load it.

      How bay 3 works

The top one holds four pads on edge35, the TV, soundbar and streaming remotes, and a USB-C lead fed from the 10-gang to charge a pad in the drawer.

      The turntable zone

      • The deck: on isolation feet, 2 cm back from the worktop's front edge, with 8.8 cm behind it for the lid's hinges. The zone takes a deck up to the size of an AT-LP120X (45.2 × 35.2 cm); most decks are smaller.
      • The lid: AT's cover is 44.1 × 34.6 cm17, so standing open its top edge is at about 121; the shelf's underside is at 130.
      • Bass: the sub is in bay 2, in the same base the deck sits on. It stands on an isolation riser, clear of the divider and the frame, and the deck stands on isolation feet. If a record skips or hums at film volume, turn the sub down for vinyl.
      • Signal path: turntable set to PHONO → the preamp under the shelf → a 2 m RCA-to-3.5 mm lead down the groove behind the left upright and along the back of the worktop to the soundbar's AUX. If the deck has no PHONO/LINE switch, plug it straight into the AUX.
      • Soundbar: Music mode, bass up, surround, night and dialogue modes off. Always the AUX cable, never Bluetooth.

      Using it

      1. Opening: clear the floor in front of it and push the ottoman to the sofa. Open the chair door, lay it back over the table door and take the four chairs out, then shut it.
      2. Open the table door and lay it back over the chair door, where a flush magnet holds it. Lift the two chairs out of the base, front one first.
      3. Pull the finger pull at the top of the folded table and lower it halfway on its piano hinge43. Unfold the inner half's two legs until each clicks44, then lower it onto them. Lift the outer half up and over, unfold its legs until they click, and lower it. The table is 185 long, its top at 76, level with the media wall's worktop.
      4. Folding away: do it the other way round. Fold the legs and the outer half, swing the table up until the catches take it, then put the two chairs in the base and shut the table door. Then the four chairs go in the chair box. Use two hands, and never fold it with anything on the table.

      The chairs: your grey padded ones

      Your chairs62: Brayden Studio's wooden folding chairs in linen, sold in pairs, a 47 × 47 seat with a 6.5 cm cushion, 168 kg each. Folded they're 90 × 10 × 47: only 1 cm thicker and 1 cm taller than the beech FRÖSVI the cabinet was drawn for, so they pack in the same way with three small changes:

      • 23.4 deep instead of 22, so two stand one behind the other (20.8 inside for two at 10). The cabinet stands 1.4 cm proud of the pipe boxing.
      • The chair box 49 wide inside (was 46), for a 47 chair: the cabinet is 147.2 long.
      • The chair shelf at 94 (was 93.5), so a 90 chair stands under it and over it with a centimetre to spare. Two still lie in the table box's base, 0.5 clear at each end.

      The listing doesn't give the open chair's depth, height or seat height, so those are drawn at a like-for-like chair's63: 61 deep, 78.7 tall, the seat at 44.5. Seated on the stair side, a chair's back reaches into the door's swing: keep the door shut while you eat unless they measure 52.3 deep or less. About £80–130 a pair.

      How it's built

      Step 11 of the build guide builds it in order, with every size. You build the two boxes and screw them together and to the wall. Then the hinge rail, the two halves with their aprons and legs, and the joint. Then you hang the table, the catches, and the two doors on their piano hinges. The drawings below are the ones to have open on the bench.

      • The two boxes: oak-faced ply, cut to size by the merchant. Each has two ends 189 tall and 23.4 deep, a top and a floor between them, a 6 mm back and a shelf set back behind the door. The table box is 91 inside and the chair box 49. They're screwed to each other through their meeting ends, so they read as one cabinet.
      • The doors: 90.5 and 48.5 wide, 183.8 tall, 18 mm oak-faced ply, about 21 and 11 kg. They're inset flush with the front edges, the grain upright, each on a 1800 mm stainless piano hinge (1.9 short of each end) on the boxes' meeting ends. A stop with a magnetic catch sits behind each free edge.
      • The hinge rail: solid oak, 91 × 16.8 × 7, across the table box with its top at 73.3, its front 4 behind the door (the cloth bag hangs on the door in front of it). The table's piano hinge sits 4.6 back from its front. It carries the table's whole weight when it's open.
      • The halves and the joint are as before: edge-glued oak with pegged breadboard ends, each on an apron frame, the legs folding flat inside on self-locking brackets, three brass flip-top hinges at the joint.

      It costs about £1,026–1,735, the chairs included: the "6 Dining wall" rows of the buy list (Buy list).

      Safety: never swing the table up or down with anything on it. Check all four legs have clicked before you load it, and let the catches take it when it's folded. Hang the table door, open it flat and check its far end doesn't drop before you load the cabinet: piano hinges don't publish a load, so that's the test.

      Light, in three warm layers

      • The LED strip on the ceiling (as now): round the room's edge, into the alcove and across the breast; 2700K on a dimmer.
      • Built into the oak (smart colour): an RGB and tunable-white strip in each upright's groove and one under the side-wall run's front edge37, in the same app as the bars' bulbs, so each scene sets them too; on their plug-in power on the 10-gang (no fused spur). The 6500K bias light on the back of the TV stays plain white: it's there for the picture, not the mood.
      • Your red lamp: the three-headed floor lamp you have, its colour bulbs green at the top, pink in the middle and purple at the bottom. A deep green room needs a low layer as well as the light from above; it's also the one to leave on for a film. It can stand in any of the three spots in the 3D room.
      • Two spot bars in the style of Dunelm's Wolston (£49 each; 84 × 16 cm, 22.4 cm drop; 4 × E14, 6 W max14) on your two existing ceiling points, both running from the TV towards the window. Bar 1 hangs on the rose straight out from the TV unit, halfway to the sofa; bar 2 on the pendant point by the stairs, along the west wall, so its end no longer comes near that wall. Smart colour bulbs: eight E14 bulbs under the bar's 6 W, the WiZ Colour P45 (4.9 W, 4.5 × 10.1 cm) or, if it shows below a shade, the shorter Philips Hue lustre (5.1 W, 4.5 × 7.7 cm)38. Smart bulbs need full power, so no dimmers: the wall switches stay as they are and stay on; level and colour come from the app (or an optional smart button). Turn them as you like: each bar turns on its rose and clears every wall at any angle (bar 2 by 5.5 cm), and each head aims on its own; tap a bar or the red lamp in the 3D room to try it.

      Where the heads point: all eight heads straight down, evenly spread along each bar, so their pools overlap into one even light over the room: that's the Bright preset, the default. Tilt a head only if its pool lands badly (in the TV's screen from the sofa, or in someone's eyes). Set the bulbs to warm white (3000K) for Bright, 2700K for Cosy, and save colours for the presets you want them in.

      Three lighting presets

      Three presets instead of six buttons: Bright (the default), Cosy and Film, each set on the strip's controller, the inline dimmer on the uprights' LED driver, and the bars' and the lamp's smart bulbs in their app. Save the three as scenes in the app (and on the smart button if you get one). In the 3D room the Lights tab has the three tiles, the evening or daytime switch, and every light's slider folded under them.

      Two rules
      • The table's open, so bar 2 lights it: on top of whichever preset is on, bar 2 comes up to at least 80, bar 1 down to 15 or less, and the TV's bias light goes off.
      • Evening or daytime is a switch of its own: daytime is the sun through the window, with any preset.
      • All eight heads straight down, spread a little along each bar, so the pools overlap.
      • The ceiling strip and the uprights fill the edges; the lamp adds a low warm layer.
      • Turn the strip down first as the evening goes on: it's the flattest light in the room.
      • Bar 1's pink head on the turntable and the Series X, blue on the record ledge.
      • The uprights' grooves up, washing the wall either side of the TV.
      • The lamp up for reading sleeves on the sofa; the ceiling strip nearly off.
      • Bar 1 off: its heads hang in front of the screen, and even tilted away they'd catch it.
      • The bias light and your red lamp do the work.
      • Bar 2 just glowing on the framed LPs, so the far end of the room isn't a black hole.

      Power

The left outlet feeds the 10-gang; the right one feeds the retro 6-way, so its own switch is now the retro switch. The 10-gang's switches sit behind the TV, where you can't reach them any more.

      Electrics: your own job

      You're doing the electrics yourselves. In England, Part P of the Building Regulations decides what needs an electrician or building control.

      • Notifiable (not for you): a new circuit, a replacement consumer unit, or any change to a circuit round a bath or shower.
      • Not notifiable (yours): the socket swapped for a double, and the two spot bars in place of the old fittings. Like for like, so no electrician and no building control.
      • Still to the wiring regulations (BS 7671), every time.
      • The light switches stay: the bars' smart bulbs need full power, so there are no dimmers to fit.
      • Not mains work at all: the Cat6 and the conduits.
      The safe routine, every time
      1. Isolate: switch off that circuit's breaker at the consumer unit (the lighting circuit for the bars, the socket circuit for the socket). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch.
      2. Lock off: fit the MCB lock-off and padlock, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board.
      3. Prove dead: check the tester lights on its proving unit, test between every pair of terminals (live–neutral, live–earth, neutral–earth), then check the tester on the proving unit again.
      4. Photograph the wiring before you disconnect anything, and connect the new one wire for wire: brown (or red) to L, blue (or black) to N, green-and-yellow to earth, sleeved, no copper showing, every screw tight.
      5. Test: power back on, then the socket tester in both outlets; each bar's four bulbs come on and join the app.
      Stop and call an electrician if…
      • the tester shows anything live after you've isolated;
      • the wiring is old (rubber or fabric sheath, or red and black with no earth), or there's no earth at a ceiling point (the spot bars need one);
      • there are more wires than you can match to your photo (two-way switching, a loop in a ceiling rose you can't follow), or scorch marks, or a loose, hot or crumbling fitting;
      • the consumer unit has rewireable fuses or no RCD;
      • a job grows into a new circuit, consumer unit work, or anything by the bath or shower.

      • The channel: 4 cm behind the frames, flat two-compartment trunking: mains on one side, HDMI, Cat6 and audio on the other. Switch 2 and the retro 6-way stand on edge in it.
      • The grooves behind the uprights: the left one takes the Series X's HDMI and power and the vinyl lead, the right one Deco B's 12 V and patch leads, down to the worktop's slot.
      • The PC: through the shelf's brush grommet into two conduits chased into the side wall (the HDMI and Cat6 in a 38 mm one, its mains lead in a 25 mm one), behind the skirting and into the plinth notch; the mains lead goes on to the 10-gang.
      • The sub: its mains lead from the 10-gang drops through the slot behind the TV to the back of bay 2, about 1 m. Keep the channel behind the sub clear: its port needs the air.
      • Airflow: console bays stay open-backed; the Series X has 15 cm each side and 21 above.

      Stage 1: the mesh up today, before any cables

      1. Unplug everything from the hub. Log in at 192.168.0.1 with the password on its base, then Modem Mode → Enable Modem Mode → Apply. Its settings page moves to 192.168.100.1.
      2. Connect a hub port to Deco A and set it up in the Deco app, reusing the old Wi-Fi name and password. If it shows no internet, try another port and restart the hub.
      3. Plug Switch 1 into Deco A's other port, then the PCs into Switch 1.
      4. Add Deco B in the living room and Deco C in the kitchen. For now they link over Wi-Fi.
      5. Check the Xbox's network settings show NAT: Open.

      Stage 2: after your Cat6 runs (step 3)

      1. Plug run 1 into Deco B's free port (Switch 2 stays in the other) and run 2 into Deco C.
      2. In the Deco app, check Deco B and Deco C show as "Ethernet".
      3. Plug the Series X, Xbox One, Xbox 360, PS3, PC and TV into Switch 2.
      4. Under QoS, give the Series X and the PC high priority; turn on guest Wi-Fi and automatic firmware.
      Cabling rules
      • Solid pure-copper Cat6, round; not CCA or flat cable for the long runs. Measure the real route and add 2–3 m.
      • Cross mains at right angles; never staple through a cable; no kinks; label both ends. Never two cables between the same two devices.
      • Done when: Deco B and C show "Ethernet", each PC shows 1.0 Gbps, the Xbox shows NAT: Open, and phones hold a strong signal in the kitchen and across the living room.

      Sound layout

      • Sub: wireless, in bay 2 under the TV, its driver facing the room and its rear port 15.6 cm from the wall through the open back (15–30 is advised25). Next to the soundbar, its bass blends with the bar instead of coming from behind you, and it's off the floor where feet and drinks are. If the bass booms, turn it down rather than moving it.
      • Rears: the soundbar's own two rears, on slim floor stands directly behind the sofa (from your photos): one at each end of its long side, in the 13 cm gap between the sofa's back and the window wall, the left one in the corner and the right one at the window end, where the curtains hang in the same gap: closed, they fall over it and muffle it, so keep that end open when you watch. Both speakers sit just above the sofa's back, at about seated ear height (96–110.4), facing the room. They're linked by a cable along the skirting behind the sofa and powered from your double socket behind the sofa's short side. In the 3D room they move in Edit room.

      ★Start here: mark the heightsSteps 1 and 5 · ½ daycheck_circle
      Five rules
      • Check every wall before you drill with the detector; never straight above, below or beside a socket or switch.
      • Measure twice, cut once. Walls are rarely square: cut to the smallest measurement.
      • Two people for anything over 15 kg: the uprights, the worktop, the table, the TV.
      • Electrics: isolate, lock off and prove dead every time. Anything new is an electrician's (chapter B's stop list).
      • Dry-fit everything before glue or screws.
      1. The alcove's width at the floor, 76, 134, 155 and 196 cm and at the ceiling: cut everything to the smallest.
      2. The floor's level across the alcove, and the chimney breast's flatness with a long level.
      3. The door's swing, and the sofa: overall width, depth with the return, back height.
      4. Count the LPs and games (PS2, Xbox 360, Xbox One), and measure ten cases of each.
      5. Make a cardboard template of the alcove at worktop height: walls are rarely square.
      Set up a datum
      1. Find the floor's highest point across the alcove (you measured its level in Start here). Every height in this plan is measured from there.
      2. Stand the laser in the middle of the room, level it, and mark a line at exactly 100 cm above that high point on the alcove's back wall, both side walls and the chimney breast.
      3. Measure every other height up or down from the 100 line, not up from the floor: the floor is the thing that isn't level.
      The alcove's heights
      1. Put a strip of masking tape down each side wall and the back wall of the alcove and mark these heights on it:
      2. 73: the tops of the frames and bay 3 (the worktop's underside).
      3. 76: the worktop's top.
      4. 130 and 134: the Series X shelf, underside and top.
      5. 153 and 155.4: the record ledge and the wrap ledge, underside and top.
      6. 192 and 196: the high shelf, underside and top.
      7. Carry the 153 and 155.4 lines along the side wall to 250 cm out from the alcove's back wall, for the wrap ledge and the PC shelf.
      Across the back wall
      1. Mark the uprights' positions from the side wall: the left one 50.5–55, the right one 181.5–186. Turn the laser to its vertical line and draw both lines from the worktop line to the ceiling.
      2. Mark the base from the side wall along the floor: filler 0–3, then bay 3 3–63, bay 2 63–123, bay 1 123–183, filler to 186.
      On the chimney breast
      1. Find the breast's centre: 58.75 cm from its alcove-side corner. Draw it plumb from the floor to 170.
      2. Mark the “now playing” ledge's top at 104, level, and its two concealed brackets 6 cm in from each side of the breast.
      3. Mark the glass display case's bottom edge at 137 and its top at 222, 90 wide, centred on the line; its oak cleat's top edge at 212. (The dining table isn't here: it's in its cabinet by the stairs, chapter 5.)
      Check for cables
      1. Run the detector along every line where you'll drill: the cleats, the spacer blocks, the upright brackets, the ledge's brackets, the PC shelf and, on the stairs wall, the cabinet's two wall brackets.
      2. Mark anything it finds in red, and compare with your own photos from chapter B. Move a fixing 5 cm rather than drill near a cable.

      Check before moving on: Every figure within 1 cm of the plan. If not, send the numbers and the drawings are redone first.

      Check before moving on: Every line level end to end, and the uprights' lines plumb.

      The plinth under bays 1 and 2
      1. Lay the two 120 × 9 rails on edge, 38 cm apart outside, and stand the three 34.4 × 9 cross-pieces between them: one at each end and one in the middle, at 60.
      2. Pre-drill, glue and screw through the rails into each cross-piece end with two 4 × 40 screws.
      3. Measure both diagonals: when they're equal the frame is square. The plinth is 120 × 38 × 9. The opening between 0 and 60 (the end nearer the side wall) stays clear: it's the hidden drawer's bay, under bay 2.
      4. Stand it in the alcove 63 cm from the side wall (bay 3 stands on the floor between it and the wall) and 4 cm off the back wall. Level it with shims, side to side and front to back.
      The BESTÅ frames
      1. Assemble both frames to IKEA's instructions, but leave the back panels off: the open backs are how the cables and the sub's port breathe.
      2. Join the two frames side by side with IKEA's connectors.
      3. Stand them on the plinth, their backs flush with its back edge, so their fronts sit 2 cm proud of the plinth (the face frame covers the step).
      Bay 3, the carcass for the LP crates and the slim column
      1. While the sides are flat, mark the runner lines on their inner faces: on the right side 2.3 and 37.0 cm up from the bottom edge, for the two LP crates; on the left side 2.3, 25.1 and 47.9, for the three slim drawers.
      2. Stand the bottom panel between the two sides, flush with their bottom edges, and the top panel flush with their top edges. Pre-drill, countersink, glue and screw with four 4 × 50 screws a joint.
      3. Check the diagonals for square. The carcass is 60 × 40 × 73, open at the back.
      4. Stand it in its place, 3–63 from the side wall, its top level with the frames' tops at 73. Shim under it if the floor drops away.
      5. Clamp it to bay 2 and fit two connector bolts at the front and two at the back.
      Fix it to the wall
      1. Screw a 4 cm spacer block to the back wall behind the top of each bay, at 68 high, with plugs.
      2. Push the whole base back against the blocks.
      3. Fit two anti-tip brackets per bay through the blocks into the wall. Do this before anything heavy goes in: a full LP crate pulled out is about 30 kg in front of the unit.
      4. Lay a level across all three tops: within 1 mm over 186 cm. Shim and re-check.
      The cable channel
      1. Lay the flat two-compartment trunking on the floor in the 4 cm channel behind the base: mains on the wall side, data on the other.
      2. Run the leads in now: the two mains leads from the side-wall socket enter through the face frame's notch and run back in the 3 cm filler beside bay 3; the Cat6 and Deco B's lead come down the right-hand corner.
      3. Keep the channel behind bay 2 empty: the sub's port breathes into it. Switch 2 and the retro 6-way stand on edge behind bay 1.
      Tools
      • Drill-driver
      • Router with a 6 mm straight bit (the game drawer's base groove)
      • Combination square
      • Spirit level
      • Clamps
      • Mitre saw or tenon saw
      Fixings
      • Runners: two pairs of 400 mm (68–70 kg) for the LP crates, three pairs of 400 mm light-duty for the slim drawers, one pair of 350 mm soft-close, one pair of 300 mm
      • 3.5 × 16 mm screws for the runners (every hole)
      • Four shelf pins for the part shelf
      • Two small steel angle brackets for the divider
      • Panel pins, wood glue, felt
      The console shelves
      1. Bay 1, from the top: rows of 16 (Xbox One), 16 (Xbox 360), then the game drawer's 25.2. Put the shelves on the pin holes nearest those heights.
      2. Bay 2: the PS3's row of 23.7 at the top, on a full-width shelf. Below it, the PS2 and the PS1 sit beside the sub (next part).
      Bay 2's sub column
      1. Stand the 12 mm divider on the bay's floor, 23.4 cm from the bay's left inner face, tight under the PS3 shelf. Check it's plumb.
      2. Fix it with one small angle bracket at the bottom (into the frame's bottom panel) and one at the top (into the PS3 shelf's underside).
      3. Drill two 5 mm pin holes in the divider's right face at the height of the frame's pin holes for the PS2/PS1 shelf. Fit the part shelf on four pins.
      4. Pair the sub with the soundbar now: its PAIR button is on the back, and it's hard to reach once it's in.
      5. Lay the isolation riser on the column's floor, its front edge flush with the frame's front.
      6. Stand the sub on it with the grille facing the room, centred: 1 cm to the divider, 1 cm to the frame's side. Slide it forward until its front is flush with the face frame's front (2 cm proud of the frame). Run its lead out of the back.
      7. Check it touches nothing but the riser. If it does, a sheet of felt between, or nudge it.
      The game drawer (bay 1, bottom row)
      1. Fit the 350 mm runners to the frame's sides, level, so the drawer's base will sit about 1 cm above the frame's bottom panel. Drill pilot holes: BESTÅ sides are particleboard. If a screw won't hold, glue a 12 mm ply packer behind the runner.
      2. Rout a 6 mm deep groove 1 cm up from the bottom on the inner faces of the sides, back and front panel, 9 mm wide, for the base.
      3. Glue and screw the box together round the base: outside 54.3 × 35. Check the width against the runner maker's figure (usually the opening less 25.4 mm) before the glue sets.
      4. Fit the cross divider 13 cm back from the front, and the two bin walls 16 cm in from each side. Glue in the bin floors with a slight back-rake, so the cases lean about 13°.
      5. Felt the base and make the follower blocks.
      6. Fit the runners' inner members to the box, hang it, and check it runs true empty.
      Bay 3: the divider, the LP crates and the slim drawers
      1. Stand the 12 mm divider in the bay, its left face 17.8 cm from the left side's inner face, the full height inside. Check it's plumb and parallel to the side at front and back (measure both), then fix it with two small angle brackets top and bottom.
      2. Mark the runner lines on the divider's faces: on its right face 2.3 and 37.0 (the crates), on its left face 2.3, 25.1 and 47.9 (the slim drawers), matching the lines on the sides.
      3. Screw the crates' 400 mm runners to the right side and the divider's right face; the slim drawers' to the left side and the divider's left face. Use every hole: a full crate is about 30 kg.
      4. For each LP crate, glue and pin the two 40 × 8 sides and two 33.1 × 8 ends on top of the 34.9 × 40 base. The trough is 33 inside: snug for 31.4 sleeves, like a record shop's crate.
      5. Glue a raked rest (an oak offcut) at the back of each crate, so the sleeves lean back about 10°. Felt the trough.
      6. For each slim drawer, glue and pin the 6 mm sides, back and front onto the 15.3 × 40 base: 14.1 inside, for 13.5 cm game cases face-out. In the top one, glue a 6 mm strip down the middle (two pads on edge each side) and drill a 20 mm hole in the back for the USB-C lead's grommet.
      7. Hang each box and run it in and out empty, then with ten records or ten games. Feed the charging lead from a USB plug on the 10-gang down the channel, with a loop of slack so the drawer opens fully.
      The hidden plinth drawer
      1. Make the box: the two 34 × 4.4 sides, the two 49.6 × 4.4 ends between them, the 6 mm base screwed underneath. It's 52 × 34 × 5.
      2. Pack the plinth's inner faces under bay 2 with ply strips so the 300 mm runners sit the box's width plus their allowance apart, and fit the runners with the box 1.6 cm off the floor.
      3. Felt the runners: the drawer sits under the sub.
      The face frame and the drawer fronts
      1. Cut the stiles (about 5 wide, and one 2 wide over bay 3's divider) and the rails from 2 cm oak. The bottom rail covers the plinth, 9 tall under bays 1–2, with an opening 54 × 6 for the plinth drawer, 1.6 up, under bay 2.
      2. Scribe the two end stiles to the walls, then glue and pin the frame to the frames' fronts and bay 3. Notch the bottom rail's left end for the two socket leads.
      3. Screw the oak lips onto the game drawer, the two LP crates, the three slim drawers and the plinth drawer from inside each box, with a 2–3 mm gap all round to the face frame.
      4. Cut each finger pull underneath its lip: a cove routed along the back of the bottom edge.

      Check before moving on: The tops level within 1 mm across 186 cm, and nothing rocks.

      Check before moving on: Every drawer runs smoothly, the two crates clear each other by 2 cm, and the slim drawers by 2.8.

      Sizes are finished sizes, length × width × thickness; a 4 mm saw cut between pieces. Ply parts can be cut by the merchant from these layouts.

      Tools
      • Hardboard or cardboard, 190 × 50, for the template
      • Compass or a pencil on a block, for scribing
      • Track saw or circular saw with a guide
      • Jigsaw
      • Router with a straight bit
      • Random-orbit sander, 120 and 180 grit
      • Drill-driver
      • A helper
      Fixings
      • 4 × 30 mm screws with washers (9)
      • Hardwax oil
      Make a template
      1. Cut the hardboard to about 190 × 50 and push it into the alcove at worktop height, its back edge against the back wall.
      2. Set the compass to the widest gap at one end and run it down the side wall, so the pencil copies the wall's line onto the board. Cut to the line. Do the other end the same way.
      3. Mark the front edge at 46 cm from the back wall all along. The template is now the worktop's exact shape.
      Cut the oak
      1. Lay the board best face up, grain running along its length. Lay the template on it and draw round it.
      2. Cut just outside the line with the track saw, then sand or plane to the line.
      3. Keep the offcut flat and oiled with the rest: it's spare oak for any repair.
      4. Chamfer the worktop's top front edge with a 3 mm chamfer, sanded by hand.
      Cut the openings
      1. The TV slot: 3 cm wide, from 1 to 4 cm in from the back edge, running 78.25–158.25 from the side wall. Clamp a batten as a guide and rout it in passes, or drill each end and jigsaw between. Push the brush strip in.
      2. The grommet hole behind the deck: 35 mm, its centre 2.5 cm from the back edge and 25.25 from the side wall.
      Finish and fix
      1. Sand to 120, then 180. Oil every face: top, underside, both ends and the cut edges of the slot. Two coats, a night between them.
      2. Two of you lift it in and push it back to the wall. It should touch both side walls along their length.
      3. Inside each bay, drill three 5 mm holes up through the top panel, elongated front to back to about 12 mm long, so the oak can move with the seasons.
      4. Screw up through them into the worktop with 4 × 30 screws and washers. They must not come out through the top: check the length against a scrap.

      Check before moving on: Tight to both walls, and the slot sits over the channel.

      Cut the uprights to length
      1. Measure from the worktop to the ceiling at each upright's position. The plan says 159; ceilings vary.
      2. Cut each upright 2 mm under its measurement, then scribe its top to the ceiling as you did the worktop.
      3. Mark each upright's faces: which side faces the TV, and the back edge that goes against the wall.
      The housings (both uprights)
      1. Measure from each upright's foot (the end on the worktop). The high shelf's housing is 116–120 up, the full 30 depth, 1.2 deep, on the TV-side face of both uprights.
      2. The record ledge's housing is 77–79.4 up, 0–7 from the back edge, 1.2 deep, on the TV-side face of both.
      3. On the left upright's other face (the turntable side), a second high shelf housing at 116–120, full depth, for the short length.
      4. Clamp a straight batten as a guide, set the router 4 mm deep and rout, then step down to 12 mm in passes. Square the ends with a chisel. Practise on an offcut first.
      The through-mortises (left upright)
      1. Two mortises, each 6 wide and 2.4 tall, at 54.8–57.2 up from the foot, 12–18 and 20–26 cm from the back edge.
      2. Mark them on both faces with a square and a knife. Drill most of each out with the 20 mm bit, halfway from each face, then chisel to the lines.
      3. On the TV-side face, flare the top and bottom of each mortise outwards 3–4 mm, for the wedges.
      The tenons (Series X shelf)
      1. On the shelf's west end (the end that goes through the upright), mark two tenons 6 wide and 2.4 thick, centred in its 4 cm thickness, 12–18 and 20–26 from its back edge, 4.5 long.
      2. Saw the shoulders and cheeks, and cut away the rest of the end back to the shoulder line.
      3. Saw a kerf 3 cm deep across the middle of each tenon, parallel to the shelf's faces.
      4. Test-fit through the mortises: snug, pushed in by hand.
      The grooves
      1. On each upright's TV-side face, rout a groove for the LED channel (usually about 1.7 wide × 0.8 deep: check yours), 2 cm in from the front edge, from 2 cm above the worktop to just under the high shelf's housing.
      2. On each upright's back edge, rout a 2 × 1.5 cable groove the full length: the left one for the Series X's HDMI and power and the vinyl lead, the right one for Deco B's 12 V and patch leads.
      3. Notch both uprights' tops for the ceiling LED strip.
      Dry-fit, then fix
      1. Lay each upright on the floor with its shelves in their housings. Check every joint closes before any glue.
      2. Drill two 10 mm holes 3 cm deep in each upright's foot, and matching holes in the worktop at the marked positions (dowel centres make this exact). Glue the dowels into the uprights only, so they can come out.
      3. Lay the Series X's and the vinyl leads into the left upright's back groove, and Deco B's into the right one's.
      4. Stand the right upright on its dowels against the breast's side. Screw it to the reveal through three countersunk holes, with plugs, and plug the holes with oak.
      5. Stand the left upright on its dowels, check it's plumb with the laser, and fix it to the back wall with the concealed brackets.
      6. Slide the long high shelf and the record ledge into their housings from the front.
      7. Screw a 30 cm cleat to the breast's side face (the reveal) for the short high shelf, and another at the Series X shelf's underside height. Slide the short high shelf in from the front onto its cleat and into its housing.
      8. Feed the Series X shelf's tenons through the mortises from the turntable side, onto its cleat. Glue the wedges and drive them into the kerfs from the TV side. When dry, saw them flush and plane: proud, they'd touch the TV.
      9. Pegs: drill 10 mm through each upright's face into the housed shelf ends, 4 cm deep, about 4 cm from the front edge. Glue in a peg and saw it flush.
      The “now playing” ledge on the breast
      1. Cut it 105.5 × 7 × 2.4 from the shelf board's offcut and glue a 1.5 cm lip along its front edge, so a sleeve stands against the wall without sliding.
      2. Mark a level line on the chimney breast at 101.6 (the ledge's underside), 6 cm in from each side of the breast.
      3. Fit its two concealed brackets to the maker's instructions, slide the ledge on, and stand three LPs on it.

      Sizes are finished sizes, length × width × thickness; a 4 mm saw cut between pieces. Ply parts can be cut by the merchant from these layouts.

      Tools
      • Drill-driver and a countersink
      • A self-centring (Vix) bit for the piano hinges' pilot holes
      • 35 mm and 10 mm Forstner bits
      • Router with straight bits and a guide
      • Jigsaw or track saw
      • Hacksaw (to cut the table's piano hinge)
      • Chisels
      • Clamps, at least four 100 cm
      • Long spirit level and a square
      • Tape measure and pencil
      • A helper for standing the boxes and hanging the table
      Fixings
      • Altro continuous piano hinge, 1800 × 50, cut to 90 (the table's foot)
      • Two Altro continuous piano hinges, 1800 × 32 × 1 mm, stainless (the doors), not cut
      • Three Lee Valley 40574 narrow flip-top hinges (1.27 × 7.0) and their screws
      • Folding, self-locking table-leg brackets, a set of four
      • Sixteen figure-8 tabletop fasteners
      • Four magnetic catches
      • A 10 mm flush magnet and two steel cups
      • A small brass cup hook (the cloth bag)
      • Two steel angle brackets, plugs and 5 × 70 mm screws for your solid wall
      • 4 × 50, 4 × 30 and 3.5 × 16 mm wood screws (the short ones for the piano hinges), 25 mm panel pins, wood glue
      • Plastic shims, felt pads, hardwax oil, 10 mm oak dowel for the breadboard pegs
      Before you start: check and mark out
      1. Measure the gap under your shelf at both ends: it must be at least 191. The boxes are 189 tall and need 2 cm to tip up into place.
      2. Mark the cabinet's footprint on the floor: 147.2 long and 23.4 deep off the wall, its stair end 45 cm short of the stair box (that strip stays clear for the stairs' foot). Its window end is then 52.8 cm short of the pipe boxing's face. Mark the line between the two boxes, 94.6 from the stair end.
      3. Your stairs wall is solid: the two brackets go in with plugs and screws. Run the detector over both spots first, as for every hole.
      4. Lay a long level along the footprint. Note the low end: the shims go there later.
      5. Oil every oak face and edge (two thin coats, a day apart) before you assemble anything: it's much easier on flat parts, and a board oiled on one side cups.
      The two boxes
      1. Each box is two ends with a top and a floor between them, a back and a shelf. Lay the ends flat, inside faces up, and mark on each: the floor's top face at 3, the top flush with the end's top edge, and a line 2 back from the front edge, full height. The shelves and the hinge rail stand behind that line; the door sits in front of it, flush with the front edges.
      2. On the table box's two ends mark the hinge rail (66.3–73.3) and the linen shelf's top face at 168.6. On the chair box's ends mark the chair shelf's top face at 95.8.
      3. Stand two ends up and fit their top and floor between them, flush at the front: glue, pre-drill and drive three 4 × 50 screws through each end into each panel's end grain. The table box is 91 inside, the chair box 49. Each floor's bottom face is at 1.2.
      4. Fit the chair shelf in the chair box, its front edge on the line, and the linen shelf in the table box 4 behind the line (a hook for the cloth bag goes in front of it): glue and three screws through each end.
      5. Measure both diagonals of each box's front: when they're equal, it's square. Glue and pin each 6 mm back (91 or 49 × 184.2) between the ends, the floor and the top; it holds the box square.
      6. Glue and screw two battens under each floor, one 1 cm back from the front edge and one at the back: that's the plinth.
      Stand them and fix them to the wall
      1. With your helper, tip the table box up and walk it onto its marks, back to the wall; then the chair box beside it at the window end.
      2. Shim under the battens until both are level along their length, plumb at the front, and flush with each other at the front and the top. Check again after a minute: they settle.
      3. Clamp the two meeting ends together and screw them to each other with four 4 × 30 screws from inside the chair box, at about 20, 70, 120 and 170 up. Now they're one cabinet.
      4. Screw an angle bracket under each box's top, in the middle, and into the wall with plugs and 5 × 70 screws. They stop it tipping; the floor takes the weight.
      The hinge rail
      1. Slide the oak hinge rail (91 × 16.8 × 7) into the table box against the back, its top face at 73.3: its front stands 4 behind the line, like the folded table's, so the cloth bag on the door's hook clears it.
      2. Glue it, then drive two 4 × 50 screws through each end into it. It carries the table's whole weight when it's open, so don't skip the glue.
      The two table halves
      1. Ask the timber merchant for two centre panels of edge-glued staves, each 83.5 × 90 × 2.7: 78.5 between the shoulders plus a 2.5 tongue at each end, and four breadboard ends 90 × 7 × 2.7.
      2. On each end of each centre panel, rout a tongue 2.5 long and 0.9 thick, centred in its thickness: take 0.9 off each face with the router against a batten.
      3. In each breadboard end's inner edge, rout a groove 0.9 wide and 2.6 deep, centred, full length. Dry-fit: flush with the panel's long edges and flat across the joint.
      4. Drill three 10 mm peg holes down through each breadboard end and its tongue: one at the centre and one 8 cm in from each side, 1.3 cm from the breadboard's inner edge. Take the ends off and elongate the two outer holes in each tongue to 16 mm along the width, so the panel can move.
      5. Glue only the middle 10 cm of each tongue, clamp the ends on and drive the pegs (glue the outer pegs into the breadboard only). Saw flush, sand to 180 and oil both faces equally.
      6. Each half is now 92.5 × 90. Chamfer the underside edges 1 cm, except the two edges that will meet at the joint.
      The aprons (the frame under each half)
      1. Lay both halves face down on a clean blanket, their joint edges together, as on the drawing of the halves from underneath.
      2. The outer half: its two long rails (86.5) run along the half 4 cm in from the sides and 3 cm in from both ends; its two short rails (78) fit between them at the ends. Glue and screw the corners (two 4 × 50 each).
      3. The inner half: the same, but its frame stops 4.6 short of the wall end (that strip rests on the hinge rail): long rails 84.9, short rails 78.
      4. Fix each frame to its half with figure-8 tabletop fasteners every 25 cm (four a rail): recess each in the rail's top edge with the 35 mm bit, screw it to the rail and then up into the top with 4 × 30 screws. They hold the top flat but let it move.
      The legs
      1. Cut the four legs 70 long from the 6.5 × 4.5 oak. They're trimmed to the floor at the end.
      2. Screw a folding bracket to the underside of each half where its legs stand (see the drawing): on the inner half against the end rail by the joint, the leg centres 8.25 cm from the joint and 32 cm in from each side; on the outer half in the two corners at the far end, centres 8.25 cm in from the end and the sides.
      3. Screw each leg's top into its bracket. Fold them: the inner half's legs fold towards the wall end, the outer half's towards the joint. Folded, each leg lies flat inside its apron frame.
      Join the halves: three flip-top hinges
      1. Turn the halves face up, their meeting edges together, flush across the top. Mark three hinges along the joint: 10 cm in from each side and one in the middle.
      2. Rout each hinge's two leaves into the two edges to the hinge's depth with a guide, square the recesses with a chisel and screw the hinges in.
      3. Swing it: open, the two tops are flush; folded, the outer half lies flat on the inner half, top face to top face, with nothing proud.
      Hang the table
      1. Cut the 50 mm piano hinge to 90 with a hacksaw and file the ends smooth.
      2. With the inner half face down, screw one leaf of the piano hinge along its wall end, on the underside, the knuckle exactly on the end edge: a screw every 10 cm, pilot holes first.
      3. Fold the outer half onto the inner half. With your helper, lift the folded table upright into the table box, its wall end down on the hinge rail, its underside facing the room, centred (0.5 each side).
      4. Screw the hinge's other leaf to the rail's top face, the knuckle 4.6 back from the rail's front. That leaves 4 in front of the folded table for the cloth bag on the door. One screw at each end first, try the swing, then the rest.
      5. Try it: it swings down to flat with its top at 76 and back up to stand in the box without touching the sides. The folded table's top edge is at 165.8, just under the linen shelf.
      The catches and the finger pull
      1. Screw two magnetic catches under the linen shelf's front edge, 15 cm in from each side, and their plates on the folded table's top edge: they hold it upright.
      2. Rout a finger pull 12 long and 1.5 deep in the underside of the inner half's apron rail by the joint, in the middle: folded, it's at the top, and that's what you pull to bring the table down. No knob, so nothing presses into the pads on the door.
      Hang the two doors
      1. The table door (90.5 × 183.8) hangs on the table box's window end and the chair door (48.5 wide) on the chair box's stair end. The two hinges sit side by side where the boxes meet, and each door opens away from the other, turning 180° to lie flat over it.
      2. Lay a door face down, its hinge edge up. Screw one leaf of a 32 mm piano hinge along that edge, centred (1.9 short of each end), the knuckle just proud of the door's face: a 3.5 × 16 screw every 10 cm into pilot holes made with the self-centring bit.
      3. Stand the door in its opening on 2 mm packers, with an even gap all round. Screw the hinge's other leaf to the inside face of the end it hangs on, the knuckle just proud of the front edge: one screw at the top and one at the bottom first, try the swing, then the rest.
      4. Hang the table door first, then the chair door. Each should shut flush with the front edges and open right back, flat against the other door.
      5. Glue an oak door stop under each box's top, behind its door's free edge, with a magnetic catch let into it and the catch's plate on the door's back: the door closes flush and stays shut.
      6. Let the 10 mm flush magnet into the chair door's face, 36.1 from its hinge edge and 100 up, and the two steel cups into the table door's face at the same height, 32.2 and 40 from its hinge edge. Whichever door is open now holds flat against the other.
      7. Screw a small brass hook to the table door's back, high up in the middle: the cloth bag (the tablecloth and napkins) hangs on it, in the space in front of the folded table.
      8. Rout an upright finger slot in each door 5 cm in from its free edge, 26 long, 2.5 wide and 1 deep, at about 92–118 from the floor; ease its edges and oil it.
      9. Open the table door flat and press down gently on its far end: it mustn't drop. If it does, check every hinge screw is in tight before you load the cabinet.
      Level the table and trim the legs
      1. Open the table door and lay it back over the chair door. Open the table: pull it down, unfold the inner half's legs till they click, lower it; flip the outer half over and unfold its legs till they click.
      2. Lay the level across it in both directions. Mark each leg where it should meet the floor so the top is level at 76, fold the legs, saw them off square and stick felt pads on.
      Load the chairs and check
      1. Lay two folded chairs on their sides in the table box's base, under the hinge rail, one behind the other: the back one first.
      2. Open the chair door. Stand two folded chairs on the chair box's floor, one behind the other, and two on its shelf the same way.
      3. Fold the table up, shut both doors and stand back: two plain oak doors, nothing on show.

      Check before moving on: The table swings down and up without touching the box's sides, all four legs click, the top is level at 76 both ways, the catches hold it folded, and each door shuts flush with an even gap and turns back flat against the other without its far end dropping.

      Before you start: the stop list
      1. Stop and call an electrician if: the tester shows anything live after you've isolated; the wiring is old (rubber or fabric sheath, or red and black with no earth); there are more wires than you can match to your photo; there are scorch marks or the old socket is loose or hot; the consumer unit has rewireable fuses or no RCD; or the job grows into a new circuit.
      2. Nothing in this step is notifiable in England: the socket is a like-for-like swap on an existing circuit, outside a bathroom. It must still be done to the wiring regulations, which is what this routine is for.
      The Cat6 runs (low voltage: no isolation needed)
      1. Measure each route on the house plan and add 2–3 m: bedroom 3, across the landing, down through the airing cupboard.
      2. Lift a floorboard in the airing cupboard. Drill a 20 mm hole through the plate below (detector first), and feed a draw rod down to the alcove's right corner. Tape both Cat6 cables and a spare to it and pull them through. Pull the kitchen run on down the same way, past the right upright's groove.
      3. Keep the Cat6 away from mains: cross at right angles, never run alongside in the same hole. Clip it every 30 cm; never staple through it or kink it.
      4. Punch each end down onto a keystone in a surface box (or crimp a plug), to the T568B colours on both ends. Label both ends.
      5. Test each run with the cable tester: all eight lights in order. Re-terminate any that don't.
      Isolate the socket circuit
      1. Tell everyone in the house you're working on the electrics.
      2. At the consumer unit, switch off the breaker for the side-wall socket's circuit (usually a ring marked "sockets"). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch instead.
      3. Fit the MCB lock-off and padlock to that breaker, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board: "Working on this circuit, do not switch on".
      4. Prove your voltage tester on its proving unit: it must light.
      5. At the socket, with it pulled forward on its cables, test between every pair: live and neutral, live and earth, neutral and earth. No reading on any of them.
      6. Prove the tester on the proving unit again. Only now is it safe to touch.
      Swap the single socket for a double
      1. Unscrew the old socket and ease it out. Photograph the wiring before you undo anything.
      2. Check the stop list against what you see: an earth (green-and-yellow) wire present and sleeved, no scorching, the cable sheath into the box.
      3. If the double needs a bigger box, chop the plaster out round the old box to the new box's outline and fit the new box with plugs and screws, the cables through its grommets.
      4. Connect wire for wire: brown (or red) to L, blue (or black) to N, green-and-yellow to the earth terminal. Two cables in the old box go into the same terminals together. Strip only enough so no copper shows outside a terminal, and tighten every screw firmly.
      5. Fold the cables in neatly without trapping them, and screw the socket on level.
      6. Remove the lock-off, switch on, and plug the socket tester into each outlet: it should show correct wiring on both.
      The PC's two conduits in the side wall
      1. Mark the route from behind the PC shelf's back corner straight down to skirting height, then along behind the skirting to the base's plinth. Run the detector along it: move it if anything shows. Never chase near the socket's cables, which run straight up, down or across from it.
      2. Chase two channels side by side, 5 cm apart: one for the 38 mm oval conduit (data: HDMI and Cat6), one for the 25 mm (the PC's mains lead). Vertical only on the wall, no deeper than the conduit needs. Wear the mask: the dust is silica.
      3. Take the skirting off along the route, fix both conduits with a draw wire inside each, and refit the skirting over them.
      4. Fill the chase with one-coat filler, sand flush, and photograph the route with a tape measure in the shot before you paint.
      Finish
      1. Mark every route on the plan, and keep the photos with it.

      Check before moving on: The socket tester shows correct wiring on both outlets, both Cat6 runs test good end to end, and every route is photographed.

      Before you start
      1. No dimmers: smart bulbs need full power, so leave the light switches as they are and keep them on. A dimmer in front of a smart bulb makes it flicker and can damage it.
      2. The same stop list as chapter B. Here, also stop if a ceiling point has no earth (the bars need one), or the rose has more wires than you can match to your photo.
      Isolate the lighting circuit
      1. Tell everyone in the house you're working on the electrics.
      2. At the consumer unit, switch off the breaker for the lighting circuit (usually marked "lights", 6 A). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch instead.
      3. Fit the MCB lock-off and padlock to that breaker, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board: "Working on this circuit, do not switch on".
      4. Prove your voltage tester on its proving unit: it must light.
      5. At each switch and each ceiling point, with the cover off, test between every pair: live and neutral, live and earth, neutral and earth. No reading on any of them.
      6. Prove the tester on the proving unit again. Only now is it safe to touch.
      Take down the old fittings, hang the bars
      1. Unscrew each old fitting's cover. Prove dead again at its terminals. Photograph the wiring, mark the switched live (the wire from the switch) with tape, then disconnect and take the fitting down.
      2. Fix bar 1's mounting plate to the ceiling over the rose between the TV and the sofa, the bar running from the TV towards the window, with screws into the joist or the plate's fixings. Bar 2's goes on the pendant point by the stairs, running the same way, along the west wall.
      3. Connect earth first (green-and-yellow to the bar's earth), then neutral to N and the switched live to L, in the bar's terminal block; any loop wires go back together exactly as they were. Tighten, tuck, and fit the canopy.
      4. Fit the smart colour bulbs and point every head straight down, evenly spread along the bar. Tilt one only if its pool lands in the TV's screen or someone's eyes. If a WiZ bulb shows below its shade's rim, use the shorter Hue lustre there.
      Power on and test
      1. Remove the lock-off and switch on, wall switches on. In the bulbs' app, add all eight, group them as bar 1 and bar 2, set warm white at about half, then save the three presets, Bright, Cosy and Film, from the lighting presets below (levels, and colours if you want them). Your red lamp's colour bulbs go in the same presets. With the table open, bar 2 comes up to at least 80 and bar 1 down to 15 (the table rule): save that as a fourth scene, Table, if your app can't do it on its own.
      The low-voltage lights (nothing to isolate)
      1. Cut the smart strip at its marks into three lengths: one for each upright's groove and one for the side-wall run. Press each into its aluminium channel under the opal diffuser; take the uprights' leads down their grooves to the strip's power on the 10-gang (smart colour).
      2. The side-wall run's strip: in its channel in the groove under the run's front edge, 1.5 cm back from the edge, the full 220 cm; its lead drops with the PC's through the brush grommet into the conduit, to the same power.
      3. Add the strips to the app beside the bars' bulbs, so each preset sets the wall's glow too: warm white for Bright, low and coloured for Cosy and Film.
      4. Clip the ceiling strip through its notches in the uprights; stick the bias light round the back of the TV on its USB port.
      5. Stand your red lamp in its spot (the 3D room shows the three), its bulbs green, pink and purple, top to bottom.

      Check before moving on: Every bulb answers the app, the presets recall, and from the sofa no spot head shows in the screen or shines in your eyes.

      Good to know: time, tools, techniques and pitfalls

      Roughly 17–22 working days spread over a few weekends, the electrics and the Cat6 included, plus the paint drying. Steps 6–11 can be split: the base and the dining cabinet first, the oak joinery once you're confident.

      Tools

      You don't need a workshop. Hire the two big tools for a weekend (a track saw and an SDS drill), or ask the timber merchant to cut the oak and ply to the cut lists: most will, for a small charge, and that removes the hardest cuts.

      Six techniques you'll use

      1. Fixing into brick. Detect, mark, drill with the SDS on hammer setting, clear the dust, push in a brown (7 mm) wall plug and drive a 5 × 60 mm screw. In plasterboard, find a stud, or use heavy-duty plasterboard fixings rated for the load.
      2. Cutting oak cleanly. Put masking tape over the cut line, score it with a knife, cut with the good face down (circular or track saw) or up (jigsaw). Clamp a straight edge as a guide.
      3. Routing a housing (a shallow slot a shelf sits in). Clamp a straight batten as a guide, set the bit 4 mm deep, rout, then step down to 12 mm in passes. Practise on an offcut first.
      4. A wedged through-tenon. Mark the 6 × 2.4 cm mortise on both faces of the upright and drill most of it out with a 20 mm bit from each side. Chisel it to the line. Saw the tenon on the shelf's end. Saw a kerf down its middle, glue it, tap it home, then drive a glued oak wedge into the kerf. When it's dry, saw it flush and plane it.
      5. Dowelling. Use a dowel jig to drill matching 10 mm holes 3 cm deep in both parts, glue the dowels, clamp.
      6. Oiling. Sand to 180 grit, wipe off the dust, rub on a thin coat of hardwax oil, wipe off the excess after 15 minutes, let it dry overnight, give it a second coat. Do the undersides too, so the boards don't cup.

      Where beginners usually go wrong

      • Cutting the worktop to the tape instead of to a template. Make a cardboard template of the alcove first; walls are rarely square.
      • Skipping the dry-fit. Gluing a tenon that doesn't fit is the one mistake you can't undo.
      • Oil on one side only. The board cups within a week.
      • Loading the LP crates before the anti-tip brackets go in. A full crate weighs about 30 kg.
      • Folding the table up with something on it. Clear it first, every time, and keep both turn buttons turned when it's up.
